lines.42: Worked baseline example (our Phase 2 reference design):
lines.44: - Tether half-length L = 320 km, so lower tip dips to ~290 km altitude at bottom of swing... wait — for an atmosphere-grazing design we want the tip much lower. For our **HASTOL-class reference design** (modeled on the Boeing/Tethers Unlimited Hypersonic Airplane Space Tether Orbital Launch study), the lower tip reaches down to roughly **80–150 km altitude**, where a hypersonic aircraft or reusable suborbital rocket can meet it.
lines.118: The center-of-mass node hosts: solar arrays (hundreds of kW in Phase 2, multi-MW in Phase 3), batteries/flywheels for eclipse and surge power, the electrodynamic reboost power electronics, command and data handling, the winch systems that adjust tether length and trim the center of mass, attitude/rotation control thrusters for spin-up and emergency damping, propellant storage for the electric propulsion system, and (Phase 3+) crew-tended servicing facilities. The hub also serves as the ballast: its mass dominates the system, and locating massive, low-value mass here (spent stages, water, slag from early construction) is encouraged because **ballast mass improves catch dynamics** — a heavier skyhook loses a smaller fraction of its velocity per catch, simplifying everything.
lines.143: - **Electrodynamic (ED) reboost** is the skyhook's superpower: run current through conductive tether segments (aluminum or copper-clad lines woven into the structure), and the Earth's magnetic field exerts a Lorentz force — thrust with **zero propellant**, paid for entirely in solar electricity. Drive current one way to raise the orbit, reverse it to lower; modulate with rotation phase to also manage spin rate. Power levels of 100 kW–1 MW yield meaningful daily momentum restoration in LEO where the field is strong and plasma is dense.
lines.145: - Sizing requirement: the reboost system must restore the momentum of one full design-payload boost within the planned inter-catch interval (initially 5–10 days, shrinking to < 1 day at maturity) with 30% margin.
lines.193: - 200–400 km class Hoytether, hub mass of order 100–300 t (assembled over many launches; falling commercial launch prices are our friend during construction — we are launch's customer before we are its competitor), tip speed initially **1.5–2.0 km/s**, deliberately modest to keep taper ratios small and tether mass affordable.
lines.218: Marginal cost per boosted kilogram = (electricity for reboost + grapple/ops wear + insurance increment + ops labor) ÷ kg. Electricity dominates and is absurdly cheap: restoring ~30 MJ/kg of orbital energy via solar-powered ED reboost at even 20% chain efficiency costs **on the order of a few dollars of amortized solar-array time per kilogram**. The marginal cost of a skyhook boost is essentially *rounding error*; the entire price the customer pays above a few tens of dollars/kg is margin available to amortize capital. Compare: chemical launch marginal cost is bounded below by propellant and expended/refurbished hardware at tens to hundreds of $/kg even for the best reusable rockets, before capital recovery.
